definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Said of the embodied one (2.25): it is unthinkable, as well as unmanifest and unchangeable.

literal: non-dharma, what is contrary to dharma

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: In Arjuna's argument, what overpowers a whole family once its dharmas perish (1.40); when it prevails the women of the family are corrupted (1.41).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Entitlement: one's entitlement is to action alone, never to its fruits (2.47).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: In adhyātmacetasā (3.30): all actions are to be renounced in Kṛṣṇa with a mind directed to the self.

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The sense of 'I' by which one whose self is deluded thinks 'I am the doer', though actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti (3.27); the one who attains peace is without it (nirahaṃkāra, 2.71).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Epithet of the embodied one: unborn, eternal, everlasting, primeval (2.20); the knower knows it as unborn (2.21).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Inaction: one should not be attached to it (2.47); action is better than inaction, and without action even the body cannot be maintained (3.8).

notes: The Gītā returns to action and inaction at 4.16–18 (outside this chunk).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: In 3.15, that from which brahman arises (action arises from brahman, brahman from the akṣara); most commentators take it as the imperishable supreme.
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: What the steadfast person whom sense-contacts do not disturb, the same in pain and pleasure, is fit for (2.15).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The contacts of the senses with their objects, giving cold and heat, pleasure and pain, come and go and are impermanent; they are to be endured (2.14).

literal: immeasurable; not an object of the means of knowledge

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Epithet of the eternal, indestructible embodied one whose bodies have an end (2.18).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Of the asat there is no coming to be (2.16); the counterpart of sat.
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Those who follow Kṛṣṇa's teaching with faith and without carping (anasūyantaḥ) are freed from actions (3.31); those who carp at it and do not follow it are lost (3.32).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna calls the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra ātatāyinaḥ, and says sin would come upon them for killing even these aggressors (1.36).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The self in which the one of steady wisdom is content 'by the self' (2.55) and in which one who has nothing to do delights and is satisfied (3.17); that which is beyond the understanding, by which the self is steadied (3.42–43, saḥ). Also used reflexively and for the person or mind (vidheyātmā 2.64; vimūḍhātmā 3.6, 3.27; ātmavān 2.45). The embodied self of 2.12–30 is called dehin or śarīrin.
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: That by which all this is pervaded is indestructible (2.17); the knower knows the embodied one as indestructible (2.21).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The embodied one is called unmanifest (2.25); beings have an unmanifest beginning and end and are manifest only in the middle (2.28).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: No one can destroy the imperishable (2.17); the knower knows the embodied one as imperishable (2.21).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: There is no bhāvanā for the undisciplined, and without it there is no peace (2.66).

notes: Glossed by the commentators as meditation or as intent absorption in knowledge of the self.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Action arises from brahman and brahman from the imperishable; the all-pervading brahman is ever established in sacrifice (3.15) — most commentators read brahman here as the Veda. The state of the sthitaprajña is 'of brahman' (brāhmī sthiti), leading to brahmanirvāṇa (2.72).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: For a knowing brāhmaṇa all the Vedas are of as much use as a well in a flood (2.46).

literal: the nirvāṇa of (or: that is) brahman

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: What one attains who abides in the brāhmī sthiti even at the time of death (2.72).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The state of the one of steady wisdom described in 2.55–71; having attained it one is no longer deluded, and abiding in it even at death one attains brahmanirvāṇa (2.72).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The understanding declared 'according to sāṃkhya' and 'according to yoga', joined with which one casts off the bondage of action (2.39); when resolute it is single, when irresolute many-branched (2.41); it must cross the thicket of delusion and stand immovable in samādhi (2.52–53); it is destroyed after the loss of memory (2.63) and becomes steady in serenity (2.65); higher than the mind (3.42) and one of the seats of desire (3.40). Arjuna asks why action is urged if buddhi is superior (3.1).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Action is far inferior to buddhiyoga (2.49); one joined with understanding (buddhiyukta) casts off good and evil deeds (2.50) and, abandoning the fruit, is freed from the bondage of birth (2.51).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The bodies of the eternal embodied one have an end (2.18); in this body come childhood, youth, old age, and so another body (2.13).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The one who dwells in the body: passes through the ages of life and into another body (2.13); casts off worn-out bodies as one casts off clothes (2.22); is eternally unslayable in everyone's body (2.30); objects turn away from it when it does not feed on them (2.59); desire deludes it by covering knowledge (3.40).

equivalents.note: Used interchangeably for the embodied one in BhG 2.13–30.
The dehin of 2.12–30 is what the commentators call the ātman; the chunk itself uses ātman for the self in 2.55, 3.17, 3.43.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The gods, nourished by sacrifice, nourish human beings in turn and give the enjoyments they desire (3.11–12).

literal: that which upholds; right order, duty

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The field of the battle is the 'field of dharma' (1.1). In Arjuna's argument the eternal family dharmas and the dharmas of the birth-group perish when a family is destroyed, and adharma prevails (1.40–43); he is bewildered about dharma (2.7). Kṛṣṇa speaks of svadharma: for a kṣatriya nothing is better than a battle in accordance with dharma (dharmya, 2.31, 2.33); one's own dharma, though imperfect, is better than another's (3.35); even a little of 'this dharma' (the yoga of understanding) protects from great fear (2.40).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The steadfast one is not bewildered by the passage to another body (2.13); the steadfast one, the same in pain and pleasure, is fit for immortality (2.15).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Pleasure and pain come from sense-contacts (2.14) and are to be made the same (2.38); the steady-minded is not agitated in sorrows (2.56); in serenity all sorrows cease (2.65).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: With rāga, set in each sense towards its object — a waylayer not to be yielded to (3.34); senses free of rāga and dveṣa lead to serenity (2.64); the one of steady wisdom neither rejoices nor hates (2.57).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The guṇas born of prakṛti make everyone act helplessly (3.5); actions are done by the guṇas, and the deluded think 'I am the doer' (3.27); the knower thinks 'the guṇas move among the guṇas' (3.28); the Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain, and Arjuna is to be free of them (2.45); desire and anger arise from the guṇa rajas (3.37).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna's venerable elders (Bhīṣma, Droṇa), whom he would rather not kill even if it meant living on alms (2.5).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The senses are to be withdrawn from their objects like a tortoise's limbs (2.58); they are turbulent and carry off the mind even of the wise (2.60, 2.67); they are to be restrained (2.61, 2.68) and controlled first when fighting desire (3.41); rāga and dveṣa are set in each sense towards its object (3.34); they are one of the seats of desire (3.40); the senses are high, the mind higher (3.42).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The objects from which the senses are withdrawn (2.58, 2.68), which the hypocrite dwells on in the mind (3.6), and towards which rāga and dveṣa are set (3.34).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Uprooted, with the eternal family dharmas, by the faults of those who destroy a family and cause the mixing of classes (1.43).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Knowledge is covered by desire, the constant enemy of the knower (3.38–40); desire is the destroyer of knowledge and realization (jñāna-vijñāna, 3.41); those who carp at Kṛṣṇa's teaching are deluded about all knowledge (3.32).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The commitment (niṣṭhā) of the Sāṃkhyas, one of the two taught by Kṛṣṇa of old (3.3).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Desire: born of attachment to dwelt-on objects, it gives rise to anger (2.62); the one of steady wisdom gives up all desires in the mind (2.55, 2.71) and the desires enter him as rivers the ocean (2.70); the Veda-delighters are full of desire (2.43). Named as the enemy, with anger, born of rajas, insatiable, covering knowledge, seated in the senses, mind and understanding, to be slain (3.37–43).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Action: one's entitlement is to it, never to its fruits (2.47); mere action is far inferior to buddhiyoga (2.49); no one remains without acting even for a moment (3.5); action is better than inaction (3.8); it binds except when done for sacrifice (3.9); sacrifice arises from action and action from brahman (3.14–15); done unattached it leads to the highest (3.19); Janaka and others reached perfection by it (3.20); all actions are done by the guṇas (3.27) and are to be renounced in Kṛṣṇa (3.30).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The commitment of the Yogins (3.3); undertaken with the organs of action, the senses controlled by the mind, without attachment (3.7).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Cast off by one joined with the understanding according to yoga (2.39); the world is bound by action (karmabandhana) except for action done for sacrifice (3.9); the wise joined with understanding are freed from the bondage of birth (janmabandha, 2.51).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The fruit of action is not to be one's motive (2.47); the wise abandon the fruit born of action (2.51); the Vedic 'flowery speech' holds out rebirth as the fruit of action (2.43).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Restraining the organs of action while recalling objects in the mind is hypocrisy (3.6); karmayoga is undertaken with the organs of action, the senses controlled by the mind (3.7).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The fault (kārpaṇya-doṣa) by which Arjuna's nature is struck when he asks Kṛṣṇa for instruction (2.7).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: One deluded by ahaṃkāra thinks 'I am the doer' (3.27); Kṛṣṇa says that by not acting he would be the doer (cause) of confusion (3.24).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The faintness that came upon Arjuna in the crisis — unworthy of the noble, not leading to heaven, bringing disgrace (2.2).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Yoga is skill in actions (yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam, 2.50).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna is told not to yield to it and to cast off petty weakness of heart (2.3).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arises from desire and leads to delusion (2.62–63); gone from the sage of steady mind (2.56); with desire, the enemy born of rajas (3.37).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The supreme compassion that overcame Arjuna on seeing his kinsmen (1.28, 2.1).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Pitiable are those whose motive is the fruit of action (2.49).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: For a kṣatriya nothing is better than a battle in accordance with dharma (2.31); happy the kṣatriyas who meet such a battle, an open door to heaven (2.32).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: In Arjuna's argument the eternal family dharmas perish when a family is destroyed (1.40), are uprooted by the family-destroyers (1.43), and those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell in hell (1.44).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The Kauravas' minds are overcome by greed (1.38); Arjuna laments being ready to kill his own people out of greed for the pleasures of kingship (1.45).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: What one should look to in acting (3.20) and what the knower seeks to bring about by acting without attachment (3.25).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The turbulent senses carry away the mind (2.60), and the mind following the roving senses carries away wisdom (2.67); recalling objects in the mind while restraining the organs of action is hypocrisy (3.6); the senses are controlled by the mind in karmayoga (3.7); higher than the senses, lower than the understanding (3.42); a seat of desire (3.40).

literal: having me as the highest; intent on me

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: One should sit disciplined, intent on Kṛṣṇa, having restrained all the senses (2.61).

literal: contact of the senses (with their objects)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Sense-contacts give cold and heat, pleasure and pain; they come and go, are impermanent, and are to be endured (2.14).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: One who restrains the organs of action but sits recalling sense objects in the mind is called a hypocrite (3.6).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The steadfast are not bewildered by the passage to another body (2.13); understanding must cross the thicket of delusion (mohakalila, 2.52); delusion (saṃmoha) arises from anger and leads to loss of memory (2.63); one who attains the brāhmī sthiti is not deluded (2.72); desire deludes the embodied one (3.40).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The sage of steady mind is not agitated in sorrows and is free of passion, fear and anger (2.56); the seeing sage is awake in what is night for all beings (2.69).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: A person does not attain naiṣkarmya by not undertaking actions (3.4).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: In Arjuna's argument the mixing of classes leads the family-destroyers and the family to hell (1.42), where those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell (1.44).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Beings follow their own nature; what will suppression accomplish? (3.33).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Objects turn away from the embodied one who does not feed on them, all but the relish (2.59).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna is to fight free from expectation and 'mine', having renounced all actions in Kṛṣṇa (3.30).

literal: free from the pairs of opposites

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: One of the qualities of being beyond the three guṇas enjoined in 2.45.
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The one who attains peace is without 'mine' (2.71); Arjuna is to fight without it (3.30).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: When understanding crosses the thicket of delusion, one reaches nirveda towards what is to be heard and what has been heard (2.52).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The twofold niṣṭhā taught by Kṛṣṇa of old: by jñānayoga for the Sāṃkhyas, by karmayoga for the Yogins (3.3).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna is told to be free of the three guṇas, which are the domain of the Vedas (2.45).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Epithet of the embodied one (2.18, 2.20, 2.21, 2.24).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The action Arjuna is told to perform; action is better than inaction (3.8).

notes: The commentators take it as obligatory (daily) rites or one's appointed duty.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The wise grieve neither for the dead nor for the living (2.11).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna fears that sin would come upon them for killing kin (1.36, 1.39, 1.45); Kṛṣṇa says refusing a battle in accordance with dharma incurs sin (2.33) and fighting with equanimity does not (2.38); those who cook for themselves eat sin (3.13, agha); Arjuna asks what impels one to sin (3.36); desire is greatly sinful (3.37).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Well performed, it is worse than one's own dharma performed imperfectly; it brings fear (3.35).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: One is never entitled to the fruits of action (2.47); those whose motive is the fruit are pitiable (2.49).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna says that when classes are mixed the ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water (piṇḍodaka-kriyā, 1.42).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The wisdom that is 'firmly established' in the one who neither rejoices nor hates, withdraws and restrains the senses (2.57, 2.58, 2.61, 2.68); carried away when the mind follows the senses (2.67). Arjuna is said to speak prajñāvāda, words of (seeming) wisdom (2.11).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The guṇas born of prakṛti make everyone act (3.5); actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti (3.27); beings deluded by its guṇas are attached to their workings (3.29); one's own nature, which even the knower follows (3.33).

literal: one who has come for refuge

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple who has taken refuge in him and asks to be instructed (2.7).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Attained by the disciplined one who moves among objects with senses free of passion and aversion (2.64); in it all sorrows cease and understanding quickly becomes steady (2.65).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: In the yoga of understanding no adverse result arises (2.40).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Gone from the sage of steady mind (2.56); senses free of rāga and dveṣa lead to serenity (2.64); set with dveṣa in each sense towards its object, a waylayer (3.34).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Desire and anger arise from the guṇa rajas (3.37).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The relish for objects remains when one abstains from them, but turns away on seeing the highest (2.59).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The resolute understanding is not established in samādhi for those carried away by desire for enjoyment and power (2.44); when understanding stands immovable in samādhi one attains yoga (2.53); Arjuna asks about the one established in samādhi (2.54).

notes: Some commentators take samādhi in 2.44 and 2.53 as the mind, or the self, in which one concentrates.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Equanimity is called yoga: being the same in success and failure (2.48); making pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same (2.38); the one who is the same in pain and pleasure is fit for immortality (2.15).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The understanding declared 'according to sāṃkhya' (2.39) — the preceding teaching on the embodied one — as distinct from that 'according to yoga'; the Sāṃkhyas follow the commitment of jñānayoga (3.3).

notes: The commentators divide on how far the Gītā's sāṃkhya relates to the classical Sāṃkhya darśana.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Perfection is not reached by renunciation (saṃnyasana) alone (3.4); Arjuna is to renounce all actions in Kṛṣṇa and fight (3.30).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Epithet of the embodied one (2.24) and, in Arjuna's argument, of the family dharmas (1.40).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arises from dwelling on objects and gives rise to desire (2.62); to be abandoned in acting (2.48, 3.9 muktasaṅga); acting unattached (asakta) one excels (3.7) and attains the highest (3.19); the knower acts unattached for lokasaṃgraha (3.25) and, knowing that guṇas move among guṇas, is not attached (3.28); one should not be attached to inaction (2.47).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Without cultivation there is no peace, and without peace no happiness (2.66); the one whom desires enter as rivers the ocean, and who abandons all desires, attains peace (2.70–71).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The embodied one casts off worn-out bodies like clothes (2.22); it is not slain when the body is slain (2.20); without action even the maintenance of the body (śarīrayātrā) is impossible (3.8).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The eternal, indestructible, immeasurable embodied one whose bodies have an end (2.18).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Epithet of the embodied one (2.24) and of brahman established in sacrifice (3.15).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Of the sat there is no ceasing to be (2.16).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: In nityasattvastha, 'ever abiding in sattva' (2.45), one of the qualities of being free of the three guṇas.

notes: Taken as the guṇa sattva or as 'being, the real'; the commentators divide.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Success, as against failure, to which one is to be equal (2.48); perfection, not reached by renunciation alone (3.4) but reached by Janaka and others through action (saṃsiddhi, 3.20).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Dhṛṣṭadyumna is Droṇa's disciple (1.3); Arjuna declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple and asks to be taught (2.7).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Confusion of memory (smṛtivibhrama) follows delusion, and the loss of memory destroys the understanding (2.63).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna, overwhelmed by grief, casts aside his bow (1.47) and sees nothing that would dispel his grief (2.8); Kṛṣṇa: the wise do not grieve (2.11), and since the embodied one is imperishable and death certain for the born, Arjuna should not grieve (2.25–30).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Those who constantly follow Kṛṣṇa's teaching with faith and without carping are freed from actions (3.31).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna sees no good in killing kin (1.31), holds living on alms better (2.5), and asks what is better (2.7) and for the one thing by which he may reach the good (3.2); by nourishing one another gods and humans attain the highest good (3.11); one's own dharma is better (3.35); nothing is better for a kṣatriya than a dharmic battle (2.31).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: In śrutivipratipannā (2.53): the understanding perplexed by what it has heard, which is to stand immovable in samādhi; cf. nirveda towards what is to be heard and what has been heard (2.52).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna asks how the one of steady mind speaks, sits and moves (2.54); the sage free of passion, fear and anger is so called (2.56).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: One who gives up all desires in the mind and is content in the self by the self (2.55); described through 2.56–72 as unshaken in pain and pleasure, free of passion, fear and anger, withdrawing the senses, free of 'mine' and 'I', attaining peace and the brāhmī sthiti.
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Pleasure and pain come from sense-contacts (2.14) and are to be made the same (2.38); for one without peace there is no happiness (2.66).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: One joined with understanding casts off both here (2.50).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna should not waver when he looks to his own dharma as a kṣatriya (2.31); abandoning it incurs sin (2.33); one's own dharma, even imperfect, is better than another's well performed, and death in it is better (3.35).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna's faintness does not lead to heaven (2.2); a dharmic battle is an open door to heaven (2.32) and heaven is gained if slain (2.37); the Veda-delighters are intent on heaven (2.43).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The seers of truth have seen the conclusion about the real and the unreal (2.16); the knower of truth (tattvavit) about guṇas and actions is not attached (3.28).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna is told to endure (titikṣasva) the impermanent sense-contacts that give cold and heat, pleasure and pain (2.14).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The domain of the Vedas (traiguṇyaviṣayāḥ, 2.45).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: In Arjuna's argument it arises when the women of a family are corrupted after adharma prevails (1.41), leads the family and its destroyers to hell (1.42) and uproots the jāti- and kula-dharmas (1.43); Kṛṣṇa says that if he did not act he would be the maker of saṅkara (3.24).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Those who delight in the words of the Veda and say there is nothing else proclaim a flowery speech aimed at heaven, enjoyment and power (2.42–44); the Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain (2.45); for a knowing brāhmaṇa all the Vedas are of as much use as a well in a flood (2.46).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: In vedavādaratāḥ (2.42): the unwise who delight in the words of the Veda and say 'there is nothing else'.
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Paired with jñāna: desire is the destroyer of knowledge and vijñāna (3.41).

notes: The commentators distinguish jñāna and vijñāna variously.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna's condition: overcome by compassion and sinking into despondency (viṣīdan, 1.28, 2.1, 2.10).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Objects turn away from one who does not feed on them (2.59); dwelling on them breeds attachment (2.62); one moves among them with controlled senses (2.64).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Here it is one, whereas the understandings of the irresolute are many-branched and endless (2.41); it is not established in samādhi for those carried away by enjoyment and power (2.44).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Action other than for the sake of sacrifice binds (3.9); Prajāpati created beings together with sacrifice, by which gods and humans nourish one another (3.10–12); rain arises from sacrifice and sacrifice from action (3.14); the all-pervading brahman is ever established in it (3.15).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: The good who eat the remainder of the sacrifice are freed from all faults (3.13).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Equanimity is called yoga (2.48); yoga is skill in actions (2.50); the understanding 'according to yoga' (2.39); one attains yoga when the understanding stands immovable in samādhi (2.53); karmayoga is the commitment of the Yogins (3.3).
Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: Arjuna is to be free of acquiring and keeping (niryogakṣema, 2.45).

Bhagavad Gītā ch. 1–3: One should sit disciplined, intent on Kṛṣṇa (2.61); the undisciplined (ayukta) have no understanding or cultivation (2.66); the knowing one acts disciplined (3.26); one joined with understanding (buddhiyukta) casts off good and evil deeds (2.50).
